newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine opposition seeks to block postal decree.
newsitem.headline: Argentine opposition seeks to block postal decree.

text.p: Argentina's opposition Radical Party on Thursday filed a lawsuit seeking to block the Peronist government's plans to privatize the state post office by presidential decree.

The sale of ENCOTESA, the state post and telecommunications company, has been a political hot potato since mid-1995, when the economy minister at the time, Domingo Cavallo, raised allegations of attempts to monopolize the Argentine postal service for criminal purposes.

President Carlos Menem is expected to sign a decree to push through the long-delayed sale within days, but Radical deputies filed a suit at the Federal Court of Administrative Disputes on Thursday, complaining it would "trample all over our legislative powers."
"We have not come to stop the privatization of the post office but to stop a flagrant transgression not only of the state of law but of parliamentary powers," said Radical Deputy Juan Pablo Baylac.
Radical Party leader Rodolfo Terragno said his party was "ready to wage a true legal battle" to stop an "unconstitutional privatization, rushed through in a climate of suspicion."
He was referring to suspicions raised by Cavallo's charges that Alfredo Yabran, a secretive tycoon in the deregulated postal sector, wants to command an Argentine postal monopoly for criminal ends.

Cavallo was dismissed last year, but he continues his campaign against corruption and against Yabran, who recently has made rare media appearances to deny the allegations and demand that he is not excluded from any tenders for ENCOTESA.
"Don't call me a mobster," Yabran said in one interview.

Economy Minister Roque Fernandez responded by assuring that the postal decree would have "no anti-Yabran clause but neither is there a pro-Yabran cause." That provoked charges from Cavallo that the government was in cahoots with Yabran.

Menem's legal and technical secretary, Felix Borgonovo, told reporters the decree could not be signed Thursday because of delays in securing the approval of the General Trusteeship of the Nation (SIGEN), the state sector watchdog.
"There won't be any news until next week," he said.
The newspaper Clarin said it had a copy of a SIGEN report that listed 30 irregularities in the proposed privatization, such as the lack of parameters on future investment and quality of services.
